ADDITIONAL SAFETY INFORMATION
LISTEN TO THE CABIN CREW
SAFETY BRIEFING
Many passengers have seen safety
demonstrations on numerous occasions.
Taking the time to watch the safety
demonstration every time that you travel
will refresh and reinforce important safety
information so that in an emergency the
information will be easily recalled.
FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELT AT ALL
TIMES TO PREVENT INJURY
You must keep your seat belt fastened at
all times. Make sure that it is low and tight
over your hips. Practise opening and
closing it. The few seconds you spend
fumbling for your seat belt in an
emergency or in turbulence can determine
whether or not you are injured. The seat
belt can be loosened after take off, but
pilots cannot predict clear air turbulence
so please keep your seat belt on. Tighten
your seatbelt again before landing and
remember on arrival to remain in your seat
with your seat belt fastened until the seat
belt sign is turned off.
INTOXICATION AND
DISORDERLY BEHAVIOUR
The cabin atmosphere is pressurised to
about 8000ft above sea level, so any
alcohol you consume will have a greater
effect on you than normal. It is against
Civil Aviation Regulations to enter an
aircraft while in a state of intoxication or
to behave in an offensive and disorderly
LOCATE YOUR NEAREST TWO
After an accident passengers who are
disoriented and dazed have been known
to head to the exit where they boarded
the aircraft. You will waste valuable time
attempting to evacuate from this exit
unless it is the closest exit to you. Before
take off and landing, it is essential that you
locate the two nearest exits to you,
keeping in mind they may be behind you.
Count the number of seat rows between
you and these exits. This is in case smoke
and/or darkness restrict your vision. Most
importantly listen to the instructions of the
Cabin Crew who are trained to check if
the exit is free of any outside obstructions
FITTING AN OXYGEN MASK
If the aircraft should suffer a rapid loss
of cabin pressure, the oxygen levels
within the cabin will decrease in a
matter of seconds. An oxygen mask will
automatically drop down from above
your head. Put it on immediately by
pulling the mask down firmly towards
you. This will start the flow of oxygen.
SPEAK UP IF YOU SEE SOMETHING
OUT OF THE ORDINARY
Don't be reluctant to report something
that you think may be a problem or
something out of the ordinary. Passengers'
actions in alerting crew can and have
been known to prevent accidents.
IN AN EVACUATION DO NOT TAKE
YOUR CARRY ON LUGGAGE
Taking your carry on baggage in an
emergency will slow your progress. The
time spent retrieving it may prevent you
or someone else from getting out of the
aircraft. The number one priority is to
evacuate as quickly as possible.
'BRACE' POSITION FOR IMPACT
The 'BRACE' position is designed to limit
the impact of forces on your body and to
help you survive an impact. Push your
lower back firmly into the back of your
seat with your seat belt fastened low and
tight over your hips. If you can reach the
seat in front, fold your arms together,
place your folded arms against the seat
back in front and rest your head on your
arms. Place your feet firmly on the floor. If *
you cannot reach the seat in front, place
your chest on your lap with your head
down. Clasp your hands around your shins
keeping your feet firmly on the floor.
Take the time and see which 'BRACE'
position shown on the front of the card
is most suitable for you in the seat in
which you are sitting. If the crew calls
'heads down, stay down', adopt the
'BRACE' position immediately and stay
in the 'BRACE' position until the aircraft
stops completely. Be aware there may
be more than one impact.
FITTING YOUR LIFE JACKET
In the cabin crew briefing you will be
shown where to locate your life jacket
(it is under or beside your seat) and how
to put it on. Make sure you do up the
buckle and pull it tight (you can refer to
the diagram on this safety card). This
will prevent the jacket from coming off
as you enter the water. Do not inflate
the jacket inside the aircraft as this will
slow down evacuation and may prevent
you from getting out of the exit. Wait to
inflate the jacket until you are through
the exit opening, just before jumping
into the water or stepping into the raft.
Please note: Infant life jackets are not
located under seats and will be handed
out by the crew.
RESTRICTIONS ON THE USE OF ELECTRONIC DEVICES
Electronic devices may affect the operation of the aircraft
instruments and systems. Please observe the restrictions listed below.

onboard the aircraft. Devices

(approximately 20 minutes)
and must be switched off
immediately the aircraft starts

anytime medical appliances
such as:
Cellular telephones, transceivers,
FM/AM radios, pocket pagers,

Video cameras*, video players,

Hearing Aids; pacemakers,
